A sanitary landfill would probably be less costly to establish and operate than an alternative such as incineration. If properly sited and operated, a sanitary landfill would cause insignificant pollution problems, whether from runoff or leachates contaminating streams or groundwater, or from dust and odors creating air pollution and nuisance problems. If not properly sited and maintained, pollution in several forms could be extreme and the landfill might degenerate into an open dump. However, regulating agencies, particularly the Environmental Protection Agency and the Montana Department of Health and Environmental Sciences, should prevent this from happening.
The acreage required for a sanitary landfill would vary directly with the level of development and resulting population crease. A rule of thumb suggested by the U.S. Public Health Service (1970) recommends that 15 acre-feet of landfill space per year be provided for each 10,000 people. Thus the acreage becomes significant only for the conversion scenario. For an influx of 5,000 people, if a landfill were designed for 20 years service at a 20 foot depth, 75 acres would be required. Presumably more than one site would be used. Landfills would be sited close to population or pollution centers, wherever these may develop. Because of siting requirements for equipment storage, truck turn-arounds, etc., the fenced acreage would probably be about 50 percent greater than the land required just for the landfill.
